It is caused by blood rushing into an overfilled or highly compliant ventricle. It is best heard with the bell of the stethoscope at the apex in the left lateral decubitus position.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: The {{c1::S4}} heart sound is heard in late diastole and coincides with atrial contraction.
hint: Associated with an 'atrial kick' into a stiff ventricle
explanation: S4, or the atrial gallop, occurs just before S1 when the atria contract to force blood into a non-compliant, stiff ventricle. This is typically seen in conditions like concentric hypertrophy from chronic hypertension or aortic stenosis. It is always considered pathological in adults. The sound is produced by the vibration of the ventricular wall as it resists the final inflow of blood during atrial systole.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: In a pressure-volume loop, the area enclosed within the loop represents the {{c1::stroke work}}.
hint: The work done by the heart in one cycle
explanation: Stroke work is the product of pressure and volume integrated over the cardiac cycle, which corresponds to the area of the PV loop. It is a measure of the external work performed by the ventricle to eject the stroke volume into the circulation. Increased afterload or increased stroke volume will both increase the area of the loop. Total myocardial oxygen consumption is proportional to the stroke work plus the internal 'tension-area' work.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: In the Jugular Venous Pulse (JVP) tracing, the {{c1::a}} wave represents right atrial contraction.
explanation: The 'a' wave corresponds to the rise in atrial pressure during atrial systole. It occurs just after the P wave on the ECG and just before the S1 heart sound. Large or 'giant' a waves are seen in tricuspid stenosis or right ventricular hypertrophy. The 'a' wave is absent in patients with atrial fibrillation because there is no coordinated atrial contraction to produce the pressure pulse.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: The {{c1::c}} wave in the JVP tracing is caused by the bulging of the tricuspid valve into the right atrium during right ventricular contraction.
explanation: The 'c' wave occurs early in ventricular systole (isovolumetric contraction). As the right ventricle begins to contract, the tricuspid valve closes and bulges back into the atrium, cause a transient increase in atrial pressure. This wave is usually small and occurs simultaneously with the carotid pulse. On an ECG, it corresponds to the end of the QRS complex.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: The {{c1::v}} wave in the JVP tracing reflects increased right atrial pressure due to filling against a closed tricuspid valve.
hint: The wave occurring during late systole
explanation: The 'v' wave represents the peak of atrial filling that occurs while the tricuspid valve is closed during ventricular systole. The pressure rises as systemic venous return enters the atrium. Giant 'v' waves are a classic finding in tricuspid regurgitation, where the blood leaking back from the ventricle during systole further increases atrial pressure. This wave ends when the tricuspid valve opens at the start of diastole.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: The {{c1::x}} descent in the JVP tracing represents atrial relaxation and downward displacement of the closed tricuspid valve.
hint: The downward slope following the 'c' wave
explanation: The 'x' descent is the drop in atrial pressure during ventricular systole. It is caused by two factors: atrial relaxation and the downward pulling of the tricuspid annulus by the contracting ventricle, which increases atrial volume. A prominent 'x' descent is seen in cardiac tamponade. In tricuspid regurgitation, the 'x' descent is often obliterated or replaced by a systolic 'v' wave.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: The {{c1::y}} descent in the JVP tracing represents the rapid emptying of the right atrium into the right ventricle.
hint: The downward slope following the 'v' wave
explanation: The 'y' descent occurs when the tricuspid valve opens at the beginning of diastole, allowing blood to flow from the atrium to the ventricle. A steep 'y' descent is characteristic of constrictive pericarditis (the 'Friedreich sign'). Conversely, the 'y' descent is slow or absent in tricuspid stenosis or cardiac tamponade, as the blood flow into the ventricle is obstructed or restricted by high external pressure.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: In the PV loop of {{c1::mitral regurgitation}}, there is no true isovolumetric phase because blood leaks back into the atrium.
hint: A condition where the valve between LA and LV fails to close properly
explanation: In mitral regurgitation (MR), the ventricle begins to eject blood into the low-pressure left atrium as soon as contraction starts. Consequently, there is no period where both valves are closed and volume remains constant. This results in the loss of the vertical isovolumetric contraction and relaxation lines on the PV loop. Chronic MR leads to increased preload and eccentric hypertrophy, resulting in a wider loop shifted to the right.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: {{c1::Aortic stenosis}} is characterized on a PV loop by very high peak systolic pressures and a thickened ventricular wall (decreased compliance).
hint: Narrowing of the outflow valve of the left ventricle
explanation: Aortic stenosis (AS) creates a significant pressure gradient between the left ventricle and the aorta. To maintain stroke volume, the ventricle must generate extremely high pressures, causing the top of the PV loop to be much taller. Over time, the resulting concentric hypertrophy decreases ventricular compliance, which increases the end-diastolic pressure for any given volume. This often leads to a narrower loop with reduced stroke volume in advanced stages.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: In {{c1::aortic regurgitation}}, the pressure-volume loop shows a massive increase in stroke volume and no isovolumetric relaxation phase.
hint: The valve leaks from the aorta back into the LV
explanation: Aortic regurgitation (AR) allows blood to flow back into the left ventricle from the aorta during diastole, which drastically increases preload (EDV). Because there is continuous filling from both the atrium and the aorta, there is no true isovolumetric relaxation. The loop is very wide due to the high stroke volume (needed to compensate for the reflux). The PV loop often shows a characteristic 'slanted' filling phase and high systolic pressures due to the large volume ejected.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: {{c1::Mitral stenosis}} is characterized by a decrease in end-diastolic volume (EDV) due to impaired ventricular filling.
hint: Narrowing of the valve between the LA and LV
explanation: In mitral stenosis, the narrowed valve orifice creates a pressure gradient that limits the rate and volume of blood entering the left ventricle during diastole. This leads to a leftward shift of the filling line on the PV loop, representing a decreased EDV. Because the preload is reduced, the stroke volume also decreases according to the Frank-Starling mechanism. This results in a smaller, narrower loop with lower peak systolic pressures.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: Ventricular filling consists of two main phases: rapid filling and the {{c1::atrial kick}} (atrial systole).
explanation: Early diastole is marked by rapid passive filling when the AV valves open. As the pressure gradient equalizes, filling slows (diastasis). Finally, atrial contraction (the atrial kick) contributes the remaining portion of the end-diastolic volume. In healthy young individuals, the atrial kick is less critical, but in patients with stiff ventricles (hypertrophy) or mitral stenosis, it becomes vital for maintaining adequate preload.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: During the phase of {{c1::reduced ejection}}, the rate of blood flow into the aorta slows down as ventricular pressure begins to fall.
hint: The second part of the systolic ejection phase
explanation: Systolic ejection is divided into rapid and reduced phases. In the reduced ejection phase, the force of ventricular contraction diminishes, and the pressure in the ventricle begins to drop. However, blood continues to flow into the aorta due to inertial forces until the pressure in the aorta exceeds that in the ventricle, at which point the aortic valve closes. This phase ends with the S2 heart sound.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: A 'cannon a-wave' in the JVP is caused by the right atrium contracting against a {{c1::closed tricuspid valve}}.
hint: Happens when atria and ventricles are out of sync
explanation: Cannon a-waves are large, intermittent pressure waves seen in the jugular veins. They occur when the atrium contracts (atrial systole) while the tricuspid valve is closed due to simultaneous ventricular systole. This is a classic physical exam finding in AV dissociation, such as complete (third-degree) heart block or ventricular tachycardia. It reflects the total lack of coordination between the upper and lower chambers of the heart.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: The width of the pressure-volume loop (EDV minus ESV) is equal to the {{c1::stroke volume}}.
explanation: The stroke volume (SV) is the volume of blood pumped by the left ventricle in one contraction. It is visually represented on the PV loop as the horizontal distance between the end-diastolic volume and the end-systolic volume. SV is influenced by three main factors: preload, afterload, and contractility. Clinically, SV is used to calculate the ejection fraction (SV/EDV) and cardiac output (SV x Heart Rate).

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: Increased venous return, such as during leg elevation, primarily increases {{c1::preload}} on the PV loop.
explanation: Leg elevation or a rapid saline bolus increases the volume of blood returning to the right heart and subsequently the left heart. This increases the end-diastolic volume, which is the definition of preload. On the PV loop, this shifts the right-hand vertical line further to the right. By the Frank-Starling mechanism, this increased stretch leads to an increased stroke volume to handle the extra volume.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: A decrease in ventricular {{c1::compliance}} causes the end-diastolic pressure-volume relationship (EDPVR) to shift upward.
explanation: Compliance is the change in volume for a given change in pressure (dV/dP). In conditions like restrictive cardiomyopathy or concentric hypertrophy, the ventricle becomes stiff. This means that for any given volume of blood (EDV), the pressure within the ventricle (EDP) is higher than normal. On a PV loop, this is shown by a steeper or upwardly shifted bottom line (EDPVR). This can lead to diastolic heart failure.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: The administration of a positive inotrope like {{c1::dobutamine}} will increase the slope of the ESPVR.
hint: A beta-1 agonist used in heart failure
explanation: Positive inotropes increase the force of myocardial contraction by increasing intracellular calcium or calcium sensitivity. This allows the ventricle to reach a higher pressure at a lower volume, shifting the end-systolic point of the PV loop to the left and upward. This increase in the slope of the end-systolic pressure-volume relationship (ESPVR) results in a larger stroke volume and a lower end-systolic volume (ESV).

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: In the cardiac cycle, the term 'diastasis' refers to the period of {{c1::reduced filling}} that occurs between rapid filling and atrial contraction.
explanation: Diastasis is the longest phase of the cardiac cycle at normal heart rates. During this time, the pressures in the atria and ventricles are nearly equal, and blood flows slowly from the veins, through the atria, and into the ventricles. This phase is most affected by changes in heart rate; as heart rate increases (tachycardia), the duration of diastasis is the first to be shortened, which can eventually compromise total ventricular filling.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: The dicrotic notch (incisura) on an aortic pressure tracing represents {{c1::aortic valve closure}}.
hint: Occurs at the start of isovolumetric relaxation
explanation: As ventricular pressure falls below aortic pressure, blood starts to flow back toward the heart, causing the aortic valve to snap shut. This sudden closure causes a brief spike or 'notch' in the aortic pressure curve followed by a small increase in pressure as the elastic walls of the aorta recoil. This event marks the end of systole and the beginning of diastole. It corresponds to the S2 heart sound.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: Venous vasodilators like {{c1::nitroglycerin}} primarily decrease preload by increasing venous capacitance.
hint: A drug commonly used for angina
explanation: Nitrates act mainly on the venous system to cause vasodilation, which pools blood in the periphery and reduces venous return to the heart. On a PV loop, this decreases the end-diastolic volume (EDV), shifting the right boundary of the loop to the left. By reducing preload, nitrates decrease the wall stress and oxygen demand of the myocardium, which is the primary mechanism for relieving anginal pain.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: Arterial vasodilators like hydralazine primarily decrease {{c1::afterload}} by reducing total peripheral resistance.
hint: Resistance against which the heart must pump
explanation: Hydralazine acts on the smooth muscle of the arterioles to cause vasodilation, thereby lowering the systemic vascular resistance. This lower afterload allows the left ventricle to eject blood more easily, resulting in a lower peak systolic pressure and a lower end-systolic volume (ESV). On the PV loop, this makes the loop shorter (less height) and wider (increased stroke volume), effectively increasing cardiac output.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: The presence of an S3 gallop is a highly specific sign for {{c1::heart failure}} with reduced ejection fraction (systolic failure).
explanation: While S3 can be normal in young patients, its presence in an adult over age 40 suggests a dilated, failing ventricle. The sound is created by the impact of a large volume of blood hitting a compliant, thin ventricular wall during early diastole. It is often associated with elevated filling pressures and increased BNP levels. Identifying an S3 is a critical physical exam finding for diagnosing and managing decompensated heart failure.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: Atrial fibrillation leads to the loss of the {{c1::a}} wave in the jugular venous pulse.
hint: The wave caused by atrial contraction
explanation: In atrial fibrillation, the atria quiver chaotically instead of contracting in a synchronized manner. Because there is no organized contraction, there is no discrete pressure increase in the atrium to create the 'a' wave. This also means the 'atrial kick' is lost, which can lead to a significant drop in cardiac output, especially in patients who rely on that extra filling (like those with aortic stenosis or diastolic dysfunction).

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: The splitting of the S2 heart sound into A2 and P2 during inspiration is called {{c1::physiologic}} splitting.
hint: The normal type of S2 splitting
explanation: During inspiration, the decrease in intrathoracic pressure increases venous return to the right heart, which increases the right ventricular stroke volume. This prolongs the ejection time for the right ventricle, delaying the closure of the pulmonic valve (P2). Simultaneously, the increased pulmonary venous capacity slightly decreases return to the left heart, causing the aortic valve (A2) to close earlier. This widening of the gap between A2 and P2 is a normal physiologic finding.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: {{c1::Fixed}} splitting of S2 is a classic physical exam finding for an Atrial Septal Defect (ASD).
hint: Splitting that does not change with respiration
explanation: In ASD, a left-to-right shunt increases the volume of blood entering the right atrium and right ventricle, regardless of the respiratory phase. This constant volume overload delays the closure of the pulmonic valve (P2) both during inspiration and expiration. Because the delay is consistent, the split between A2 and P2 does not change with the breath cycle. This is a hallmark sign used to distinguish ASD from other causes of systolic murmurs.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: {{c1::Paradoxical}} splitting of S2 occurs when P2 precedes A2, and the split disappears during inspiration.
explanation: Paradoxical splitting is caused by a delay in the closure of the aortic valve (A2), such that it occurs after the pulmonic valve (P2). This is seen in conditions like left bundle branch block (LBBB) or severe aortic stenosis. During inspiration, the normal delay of P2 moves it closer to the already-delayed A2, causing the split to narrow or vanish. During expiration, the split becomes audible as P2 occurs earlier while A2 remains late.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: The rapid increase in ventricular pressure during isovolumetric contraction is the most {{c1::oxygen}}-consuming phase of the cardiac cycle.
hint: The heart uses the most energy here
explanation: Building up the pressure necessary to open the aortic valve requires significant metabolic energy. Myocardial oxygen consumption is determined primarily by wall stress, heart rate, and contractility. The 'pressure work' (isovolumetric contraction and maintaining pressure during ejection) is far more oxygen-expensive than the 'volume work' (the actual ejection of blood). This is why lowering afterload is so effective in treating myocardial ischemia.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: On the PV loop, the mitral valve opens at the end of the {{c1::isovolumetric relaxation}} phase.
hint: The start of diastole's filling phase
explanation: Isovolumetric relaxation ends when the falling pressure in the left ventricle drops below the pressure in the left atrium. At this crossover point, the mitral valve is pushed open, allowing ventricular filling to begin. In a healthy heart, this occurs at the end-systolic volume. If the mitral valve is stenotic, the opening may be delayed and accompanied by an 'opening snap.'

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: The ejection fraction (EF) is calculated as {{c1::Stroke Volume / End-Diastolic Volume}}.
explanation: The ejection fraction is the percentage of the blood in the ventricle that is pumped out with each beat. A normal EF is typically between 55% and 70%. It is a key clinical measure used to categorize heart failure into 'heart failure with reduced EF' (HFrEF, systolic) or 'heart failure with preserved EF' (HFpEF, diastolic). It can be calculated from PV loop parameters as (EDV - ESV) / EDV.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: Kussmaul sign is an abnormal increase in JVP during {{c1::inspiration}}.
explanation: Normally, JVP should drop during inspiration because the negative intrathoracic pressure sucks blood into the heart. In Kussmaul sign, the right ventricle cannot expand to accommodate the increased venous return (due to constrictive pericarditis or restrictive cardiomyopathy). As a result, the pressure backs up into the jugular veins, causing them to distend during inspiration. This is a classic sign of impaired right-sided diastolic filling.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: The 'v' wave in the JVP of a patient with {{c1::tricuspid regurgitation}} is often described as 'giant'.
hint: Backflow through the right AV valve
explanation: In tricuspid regurgitation, the right ventricle ejects blood backward into the right atrium during systole. Since the 'v' wave normally represents passive atrial filling from the vena cavae, the addition of regurgitant blood from the ventricle creates a massive increase in atrial pressure. This creates a large, prominent systolic 'v' wave that can often be seen across the room on physical examination. This finding is often associated with a pulsatile liver.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: In the pressure-volume loop, the {{c1::bottom-left}} point represents the opening of the mitral valve.
explanation: The PV loop is typically read counter-clockwise. The bottom-left corner is the point of minimum pressure and minimum volume (End-Systolic Volume). Once the ventricular pressure falls below the atrial pressure at this point, the mitral valve opens, and the horizontal filling phase begins. This transition marks the end of isovolumetric relaxation and the start of ventricular diastole.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: A negative inotropic effect, such as from a {{c1::beta-blocker}} or calcium channel blocker, decreases the ESPVR slope.
hint: Class of drugs that slows the heart and reduces force
explanation: Negative inotropes reduce the contractility of the myocardium. On a PV loop, this results in a rightward and downward shift of the end-systolic point, meaning the ventricle cannot generate as much pressure for a given volume. This leads to a higher end-systolic volume (ESV) and a lower stroke volume. While this may seem counterintuitive in heart failure, beta-blockers are used long-term to protect the heart from catecholamine toxicity and improve survival.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: The {{c1::isovolumetric contraction}} phase is the first phase of ventricular systole and follows the closure of the AV valves.
hint: Phase where pressure rises but volume is constant
explanation: Once the mitral and tricuspid valves close (S1), the ventricles are closed chambers. As the myocardium contracts, the internal pressure rises extremely rapidly. This phase is characterized by a vertical line going upward on the PV loop. It lasts until the ventricular pressure exceeds the pressure in the aorta/pulmonary artery, forcing the semilunar valves to open. This phase is brief but consumes a high amount of myocardial oxygen.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: Total peripheral resistance is the primary clinical determinant of {{c1::afterload}} for the left ventricle.
explanation: Afterload is the 'load' the heart must work against to eject blood. While it is formally defined by the LaPlace law (wall stress), it is most easily conceptualized as the systemic vascular resistance (SVR) or the mean arterial pressure. High afterload (as in hypertension) forces the heart to work harder during the isovolumetric phase and limits the total amount of blood ejected during the systolic phase, which can lead to hypertrophy over time.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: The aortic valve is best auscultated at the {{c1::right 2nd}} intercostal space at the sternal border.
hint: Specific anatomical location for the aortic area.
explanation: The right second intercostal space is the traditional location for listening to the aortic component of the second heart sound and murmurs like aortic stenosis. While the valve itself is deeper, the flow of blood from the left ventricle into the ascending aorta carries the sound to this specific surface location. It is part of the standard four-point auscultation exam used to isolate valvular pathology. Proper positioning of the stethoscope here allows for the clearest detection of ejection clicks or crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmurs.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: The pulmonic valve is best heard at the {{c1::left 2nd}} intercostal space at the sternal border.
hint: Specific anatomical location for the pulmonic area.
explanation: The left second intercostal space corresponds to the pulmonic area, where sounds from the pulmonary valve are most audible. This area is critical for evaluating the splitting of the S2 heart sound, as the pulmonic component (P2) is usually softer than the aortic component (A2). Murmurs such as pulmonic stenosis or pulmonary regurgitation are typically loudest at this site. Additionally, it is a key area to assess for the increased intensity of P2 seen in patients with pulmonary hypertension.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: The tricuspid valve is best auscultated at the {{c1::left 4th or 5th}} intercostal space at the sternal border.
hint: Specific anatomical location for the tricuspid area.
explanation: The tricuspid area is located along the lower left sternal border, usually in the fourth or fifth intercostal space. This site is ideal for detecting holosystolic murmurs associated with tricuspid regurgitation or the harsh holosystolic murmur of a ventricular septal defect (VSD). Because the tricuspid valve is a right-sided structure, murmurs heard here often increase in intensity during inspiration (Carvallo sign). It is also the region where the S1 sound may be split into mitral and tricuspid components in certain physiological or pathological states.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: The mitral valve is best heard at the {{c1::apex (5th intercostal space, midclavicular line)}}.
hint: Specific anatomical location for the mitral area.
explanation: The mitral area, or the cardiac apex, is the optimal location for hearing sounds generated by the mitral valve, including the S1 sound and murmurs like mitral stenosis or mitral regurgitation. This location corresponds to the point of maximal impulse (PMI), where the left ventricle is closest to the chest wall. In clinical practice, placing the patient in the left lateral decubitus position brings the apex even closer to the chest wall, enhancing the detection of low-pitched sounds like S3, S4, or the mid-diastolic rumble of mitral stenosis. It is the most lateral and inferior of the standard auscultation points.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: The first heart sound (S1) is produced by the closure of the {{c1::mitral and tricuspid}} valves.
explanation: S1 marks the beginning of ventricular systole and occurs when the pressure within the ventricles exceeds the pressure in the atria, causing the AV valves to snap shut. The mitral valve typically closes slightly before the tricuspid valve, though they are usually heard as a single sound. S1 is loudest at the apex and coincides with the carotid pulse. Conditions that increase the force of contraction or shorten the PR interval can result in a louder S1, whereas a long PR interval or reduced contractility can soften it.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: The second heart sound (S2) is produced by the closure of the {{c1::aortic and pulmonic}} valves.
explanation: S2 signifies the end of ventricular systole and the beginning of diastole, occurring when the pressures in the great vessels exceed the pressures in the relaxing ventricles. It consists of two components: A2 (aortic) and P2 (pulmonic). Under normal physiological conditions, A2 precedes P2 because the left side of the heart finishes contraction slightly earlier. S2 is best heard at the base of the heart (the upper sternal borders). Changes in the timing of these valve closures can lead to various forms of S2 splitting, which provide important diagnostic clues for congenital and valvular diseases.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: An S3 heart sound occurs during the {{c1::early diastole (rapid filling phase)}} of the cardiac cycle.
hint: Timing and mechanism of the third heart sound.
explanation: S3 is a low-pitched sound heard shortly after S2 during the phase of rapid ventricular filling. It is caused by blood rushing into a highly compliant or overfilled ventricle, creating vibrations in the ventricular wall. While S3 can be normal in children, young adults, and pregnant women, in older adults it often indicates volume overload, such as in congestive heart failure or severe mitral regurgitation. It is classically associated with 'dilated' pathology where the ventricle is stretched. The sound follows the 'Kentucky' rhythm (S1-S2-S3).

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: An S4 heart sound occurs during {{c1::late diastole (atrial kick)}} and is always pathological in adults.
hint: Timing and mechanism of the fourth heart sound.
explanation: S4, also known as an atrial gallop, occurs just before S1 when the atria contract to force blood into a non-compliant, stiff ventricle. This stiffness is typically the result of ventricular hypertrophy (from hypertension or aortic stenosis) or restrictive cardiomyopathy. The sound is produced by the sudden deceleration of blood as it hits the rigid ventricular wall. It follows the 'Tennessee' rhythm (S4-S1-S2) and is best heard with the bell at the apex. Because it requires atrial contraction, S4 is notably absent in patients with atrial fibrillation.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: During inspiration, the intensity of {{c1::right-sided}} murmurs typically increases.
hint: Directional effect of inspiration on heart sounds.
explanation: Inspiration creates negative intrathoracic pressure, which increases venous return to the right atrium and right ventricle. This increased volume results in higher flow across the tricuspid and pulmonic valves, thereby Loudening murmurs like tricuspid regurgitation or pulmonic stenosis. This phenomenon is known as Carvallo's sign and is a key clinical tool to differentiate right-sided murmurs from left-sided ones. Left-sided murmurs generally do not increase or may slightly decrease during inspiration because the expanded lungs hold more blood, slightly reducing return to the left heart.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: The Valsalva maneuver (Phase II) {{c1::decreases}} the intensity of most murmurs, EXCEPT for HOCM and MVP.
hint: General effect of decreased preload on murmur intensity.
explanation: During the strain phase of the Valsalva maneuver, intrathoracic pressure rises significantly, which compresses the vena cava and sharply reduces venous return (preload) to the heart. For most murmurs, such as aortic stenosis or mitral regurgitation, the decreased stroke volume results in less turbulence and a softer sound. However, in Hypertrophic Obstructive Cardiomyopathy (HOCM), less volume in the LV allows the hypertrophied septum and mitral valve to approximate more easily, increasing obstruction and Loudening the murmur. Similarly, in Mitral Valve Prolapse (MVP), the reduced volume causes the valve to prolapse earlier, making the murmur and click more prominent.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: A {{c1::handgrip}} maneuver increases afterload and typically increases the intensity of MR, VSD, and AR murmurs.
hint: Maneuver that increases systemic vascular resistance.
explanation: The sustained handgrip maneuver increases systemic vascular resistance (afterload) by compressing peripheral arteries. This higher pressure in the aorta opposes the forward flow of blood from the left ventricle. Consequently, more blood is forced backward through a regurgitant mitral valve (MR) or through a ventricular septal defect (VSD), Loudening those murmurs. It also increases the backward flow into the LV during diastole in aortic regurgitation (AR). Conversely, because it increases LV volume and pressure, it typically softens the murmurs of aortic stenosis and HOCM.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: Rapid squatting {{c1::increases}} both preload and afterload.
hint: Combined hemodynamic effect of this position change.
explanation: Squatting increases preload by compressing the leg veins and forcing blood back toward the heart, and it increases afterload by kinking the femoral arteries. The increased venous return and systemic resistance lead to a larger left ventricular volume. This increased volume helps 'push' the septum away from the mitral valve in HOCM, decreasing the obstruction and softening the murmur. For MVP, the increased volume delays the prolapse, making the click occur later and the murmur shorter/softer. Most other murmurs, like AS or MR, will get louder due to the overall increase in blood flow.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: In Hypertrophic Obstructive Cardiomyopathy (HOCM), standing from a squatting position will {{c1::increase}} the intensity of the murmur.
hint: Effect of sudden preload reduction on HOCM.
explanation: Standing causes a rapid decrease in venous return (preload) due to blood pooling in the lower extremities. In HOCM, a smaller left ventricular volume allows the asymmetric septal hypertrophy to encroach further into the left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT). This increases the degree of subaortic obstruction and the velocity of blood flow, resulting in a louder crescendo-decrescendo murmur. This is a classic board question because HOCM and MVP are the rare murmurs that behave 'oppositely' to most others when preload is decreased.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: Aortic stenosis is characterized by a {{c1::crescendo-decrescendo}} systolic murmur that radiates to the carotids.
hint: Shape and radiation of the most common systolic murmur.
explanation: Aortic stenosis (AS) creates a 'diamond-shaped' murmur that begins after S1, peaks in mid-systole, and ends before S2. The sound is caused by turbulent flow through a narrowed aortic orifice. The high-velocity jet of blood is directed toward the neck, which is why the murmur classically radiates to the carotid arteries. As the stenosis becomes more severe, the peak of the murmur occurs later in systole. It is often accompanied by a weak, delayed pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus) and a soft or paradoxical S2.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: Mitral regurgitation is a {{c1::holosystolic}} murmur that typically radiates to the axilla.
hint: Timing and radiation of this left-sided regurgitant murmur.
explanation: Mitral regurgitation (MR) occurs when the mitral valve fails to close completely during systole, allowing blood to flow backward into the left atrium. Because the pressure gradient between the LV and LA remains high throughout the entire systolic phase, the murmur is holosystolic (constant intensity from S1 to S2). The murmur is best heard at the apex and, due to the orientation of the mitral valve, the sound typically radiates to the left axilla. Common causes include mitral valve prolapse, ischemic heart disease, or dilated cardiomyopathy.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: The murmur of Mitral Valve Prolapse (MVP) is characterized by a {{c1::midsystolic click}} followed by a systolic murmur.
explanation: MVP occurs when the mitral valve leaflets bulge into the left atrium during systole. The 'click' is caused by the sudden tensing of the chordae tendineae as the leaflets reach their limit of displacement. Following the click, a systolic murmur of regurgitation is often heard. Maneuvers that decrease preload (like standing or Valsalva) cause the click to occur earlier in systole because the smaller LV volume allows the valve to prolapse sooner. Conversely, increasing preload (squatting) delays the click and shortens the murmur.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: A ventricular septal defect (VSD) produces a {{c1::harsh holosystolic}} murmur best heard at the tricuspid area.
hint: Sound quality and location of this congenital shunt.
explanation: A VSD allows blood to flow from the high-pressure left ventricle to the lower-pressure right ventricle. This creates a high-velocity, turbulent jet that is heard throughout systole. The murmur is typically 'harsh' in quality and is loudest at the lower left sternal border (tricuspid area). Interestingly, smaller VSDs often produce louder, harsher murmurs because of the higher pressure gradient and greater turbulence created by a restrictive opening, whereas large VSDs may be quieter because the pressures between the two ventricles equalize.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: Aortic regurgitation (AR) presents as a high-pitched {{c1::decrescendo}} diastolic murmur.
hint: Timing and shape of the murmur caused by aortic valve incompetence.
explanation: Aortic regurgitation occurs when the aortic valve fails to seal during diastole, allowing blood to leak back from the aorta into the left ventricle. The murmur begins immediately after S2 when the pressure in the aorta is highest and gradually tapers off as the pressure gradient decreases. It is best heard at the left sternal border with the patient sitting up and leaning forward, especially after full expiration. Chronic AR leads to a wide pulse pressure and hyperdynamic circulation (e.g., Water-hammer pulse).

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: Mitral stenosis (MS) is characterized by an {{c1::opening snap}} followed by a mid-diastolic rumble.
hint: The unique diastolic sound associated with rheumatic heart disease.
explanation: Mitral stenosis is most commonly caused by rheumatic heart disease. The 'opening snap' (OS) is a high-pitched sound heard shortly after S2, caused by the sudden tensing of the stenotic mitral valve leaflets as they reach their maximum opening. The rumble that follows is due to turbulent flow through the narrowed orifice during the diastolic filling phases. A shorter S2-to-OS interval indicates more severe stenosis because higher left atrial pressures cause the valve to snap open earlier. The rumble often has a 'presystolic accentuation' if the patient is in sinus rhythm.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) produces a {{c1::continuous machine-like}} murmur.
hint: The characteristic sound of a persistent fetal connection.
explanation: A PDA is a persistent connection between the aorta and the pulmonary artery. Because the pressure in the aorta is higher than the pressure in the pulmonary artery throughout both systole and diastole, blood flows continuously through the shunt. This creates a murmur that does not stop at S2, often described as 'machine-like.' It is loudest at the left infraclavicular area. It is commonly associated with congenital rubella infection and can be closed using prostaglandin inhibitors like indomethacin in neonates.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: {{c1::Fixed splitting}} of S2 is the classic auscultatory finding of an Atrial Septal Defect (ASD).
hint: S2 pattern that does not change with respiration.
explanation: In an ASD, the left-to-right shunt increases the volume of blood in the right atrium and right ventricle. This chronic volume overload delays the closure of the pulmonic valve (P2). Because the communication between the atria equalizes the effects of respiratory pressure changes on venous return to both the left and right sides of the heart, the delay in P2 remains constant throughout the respiratory cycle. This results in an S2 split that does not close during expiration, which is a hallmark finding of an ASD.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: Paradoxical splitting of S2 is seen when {{c1::P2 occurs before A2}}.
hint: The order of valve closure in paradoxical splitting.
explanation: Normally, A2 precedes P2. Paradoxical splitting occurs when the closure of the aortic valve is significantly delayed, often due to left bundle branch block (LBBB) or severe aortic stenosis. In these cases, A2 happens after P2. During inspiration, the normal delay of P2 moves it closer to the delayed A2, causing the split to disappear or narrow. During expiration, P2 moves earlier, making the split audible. This is 'paradoxical' because the split is heard during expiration rather than inspiration, which is the opposite of the normal physiological pattern.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: The {{c1::bell}} of the stethoscope is best used for hearing low-pitched sounds like S3, S4, and the rumble of mitral stenosis.
hint: Stethoscope part used for low frequencies.
explanation: The bell of the stethoscope is designed to pick up low-frequency vibrations. It should be applied lightly to the skin; pressing too hard effectively turns the skin into a diaphragm, which filters out low-pitched sounds. Clinical pearls for USMLE include using the bell at the apex in the left lateral decubitus position to identify S3/S4 or the mid-diastolic rumble of mitral stenosis. In contrast, the diaphragm is better for high-pitched sounds like S1, S2, and most regurgitant murmurs.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: The {{c1::diaphragm}} of the stethoscope is best used for hearing high-pitched sounds like S1, S2, and the murmurs of AR and MR.
hint: Stethoscope part used for high frequencies.
explanation: The diaphragm is the larger, flat side of the stethoscope head and is designed to filter out low-frequency sounds while highlighting high-frequency ones. This makes it ideal for evaluating the standard heart sounds (S1 and S2) and most systolic murmurs. It is also particularly useful for hearing the high-pitched, blowing diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation at the left sternal border. Proper technique involves pressing the diaphragm firmly against the chest wall to maximize the transmission of high-frequency vibrations.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: In patients with Mitral Stenosis, a {{c1::shorter}} S2-to-opening snap (OS) interval indicates increased severity.
hint: How the OS-S2 timing relates to disease progression.
explanation: The opening snap in mitral stenosis occurs when the pressure in the left atrium exceeds the pressure in the left ventricle at the start of diastole, forcing the stiff mitral valve open. As the stenosis worsens, the left atrial pressure (LAP) becomes chronically higher. A higher LAP means the pressure crossover point (where LAP > LV pressure) occurs earlier in the relaxation phase of the ventricle, leading to an earlier opening snap. Therefore, the closer the snap is to S2, the more severe the stenosis is likely to be.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: Tricuspid regurgitation can be distinguished from mitral regurgitation because TR intensity increases with {{c1::inspiration}}.
hint: Maneuver that differentiates right vs left holosystolic murmurs.
explanation: Both tricuspid regurgitation (TR) and mitral regurgitation (MR) produce holosystolic murmurs, making them difficult to distinguish based on timing alone. However, TR is a right-sided murmur. During inspiration, the drop in intrathoracic pressure increases venous return to the right heart, increasing the volume of blood that regurgitates through the tricuspid valve and Loudening the murmur. This is known as Carvallo's sign. MR, being left-sided, typically does not show this increase and may even slightly decrease in intensity as blood is sequestered in the lungs.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: Hypertrophic Obstructive Cardiomyopathy (HOCM) murmur intensity {{c1::decreases}} with leg elevation or squatting.
hint: Effect of increased preload on HOCM obstruction.
explanation: Leg elevation and squatting both increase venous return (preload) to the heart. In HOCM, the primary pathology is a hypertrophied interventricular septum that obstructs the left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT). When the left ventricle is filled with more blood (increased preload), the cavity size increases, which physically pushes the septum and the mitral valve apart. This wider LVOT reduces the obstruction and the velocity of blood flow, thereby decreasing the intensity of the crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: The murmur of aortic regurgitation is best heard when the patient is {{c1::leaning forward}} and at end-expiration.
hint: Optimal physical position for detecting AR.
explanation: Aortic regurgitation (AR) produces a high-pitched, blowing diastolic murmur. Leaning the patient forward brings the aortic root and the left ventricular outflow tract closer to the anterior chest wall, which enhances sound transmission. Instructing the patient to breathe out fully and hold it (end-expiration) minimizes the distance between the heart and the chest wall by reducing lung volume. These maneuvers are specific clinical techniques used to identify subtle or early-stage aortic insufficiency that might be missed during a standard exam.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: The murmur of mitral stenosis is best heard with the patient in the {{c1::left lateral decubitus}} position.
hint: Optimal physical position for detecting MS.
explanation: Mitral stenosis (MS) produces a low-pitched diastolic rumble that can be very faint. By placing the patient in the left lateral decubitus position, the cardiac apex (where the mitral valve sounds are loudest) is shifted closer to the chest wall. Using the bell of the stethoscope at the apex in this position maximizes the clinician's ability to hear the low-frequency rumble. This maneuver is essential for the physical diagnosis of rheumatic mitral disease and is a common Step 1 clinical vignette detail.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: Amyl nitrite is a vasodilator that {{c1::decreases}} afterload, which increases the intensity of an AS murmur but decreases MR.
hint: Pharmacological maneuver and its effect on afterload.
explanation: Amyl nitrite is a rapid-acting vasodilator that primarily reduces systemic vascular resistance (afterload). For aortic stenosis (AS), the reduced afterload allows the left ventricle to eject blood more quickly and forcefully across the stenotic valve, Loudening the murmur. For mitral regurgitation (MR), however, the decreased afterload provides a lower-resistance path for blood to flow forward into the aorta, meaning less blood is forced backward into the atrium, which softens the murmur. This is the opposite effect of the handgrip maneuver.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: Widened splitting of S2, where the split is heard during both inspiration and expiration (but wider in inspiration), is seen in {{c1::pulmonic stenosis}} or RBBB.
hint: Condition that causes delayed RV emptying.
explanation: Widened splitting occurs when the closure of the pulmonic valve (P2) is chronically delayed. In Pulmonic Stenosis, it takes longer for the right ventricle to eject its volume through the narrowed valve. In Right Bundle Branch Block (RBBB), the electrical signal to the RV is delayed, delaying the onset of contraction. In both cases, P2 occurs much later than A2. While the split still widens during inspiration (due to increased venous return), the baseline delay is so significant that the split remains audible even during expiration.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: The Austin Flint murmur is a mid-diastolic rumble associated with severe {{c1::aortic regurgitation}}.
hint: Murmur named after a person, caused by a jet hitting a valve leaflet.
explanation: The Austin Flint murmur occurs in severe aortic regurgitation when the regurgitant jet from the aorta strikes the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve. This causes the mitral valve to partially close or vibrate during diastole, creating a sound that mimics mitral stenosis (a mid-diastolic rumble). It is distinguished from true mitral stenosis by the absence of an opening snap and the presence of other clinical signs of AR, such as a wide pulse pressure. It represents functional, rather than structural, mitral narrowing.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: The Graham Steell murmur is a high-pitched diastolic decrescendo murmur associated with {{c1::pulmonary hypertension}}.
hint: Murmur caused by secondary pulmonic regurgitation.
explanation: The Graham Steell murmur is effectively the murmur of pulmonary regurgitation (PR) occurring in the setting of severe pulmonary hypertension. High pressures in the pulmonary artery cause the pulmonic valve ring to dilate, leading to valve incompetence. It is heard at the left sternal border and sounds almost identical to aortic regurgitation. However, it can be differentiated by clinical signs of right heart failure and the absence of peripheral 'bounding' pulses that would characterize aortic disease. It typically increases in intensity with inspiration.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: During the Valsalva maneuver, the Mitral Valve Prolapse (MVP) click occurs {{c1::earlier}} in systole.
hint: Timing change of the click when preload drops.
explanation: The timing of the MVP click is dependent on left ventricular volume. The Valsalva maneuver (Phase II) decreases venous return, leading to a smaller LV volume. With less blood in the chamber, the mitral valve leaflets are relatively 'too large' for the space and reach their limit of prolapse much sooner after the start of contraction. Consequently, the mid-systolic click shifts toward S1 (earlier), and the subsequent regurgitant murmur becomes longer in duration. This is a high-yield dynamic auscultatory finding for differentiating MVP from other systolic sounds.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: In a normal physiological S2 split, the split is only heard during {{c1::inspiration}}.
hint: Respiratory phase where P2 is normally delayed.
explanation: During inspiration, the decrease in intrathoracic pressure increases venous return to the right ventricle, which prolongs the ejection time of the RV and delays the closure of the pulmonic valve (P2). Simultaneously, the capacity of the pulmonary vessels increases, slightly reducing flow to the left heart and causing the aortic valve (A2) to close slightly earlier. These two effects 'split' the S2 sound. During expiration, the RV ejection time shortens and P2 occurs earlier, merging with A2 into a single sound. This is considered a normal, healthy finding.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: Systolic murmurs occur between {{c1::S1 and S2}}.
hint: Heart sounds that bound the systolic phase.
explanation: Systole is the period of ventricular contraction and blood ejection. It begins with the closure of the AV valves (S1) and ends with the closure of the semilunar valves (S2). Murmurs occurring in this window are 'systolic' and include aortic/pulmonic stenosis (ejection) and mitral/tricuspid regurgitation or VSD (holosystolic). Identifying whether a murmur is systolic or diastolic is the first and most critical step in auscultatory diagnosis, usually done by palpating the carotid pulse simultaneously (the pulse occurs during systole).

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: Diastolic murmurs occur between {{c1::S2 and S1}}.
hint: Heart sounds that bound the diastolic phase.
explanation: Diastole is the period of ventricular relaxation and filling. It begins with the closure of the semilunar valves (S2) and ends with the closure of the AV valves (S1). Diastolic murmurs are almost always pathological and include aortic/pulmonic regurgitation (early decrescendo) and mitral/tricuspid stenosis (mid-to-late rumble). Because diastole is usually longer than systole (at normal heart rates), the gap between S2 and S1 is longer than the gap between S1 and S2, which helps in clinical identification.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: The ejection click of aortic stenosis is a high-pitched sound heard shortly after {{c1::S1}}.
hint: Timing of the sound produced by the opening of a stiff aortic valve.
explanation: An ejection click is produced by the sudden opening of a deformed but mobile semilunar valve, most commonly seen in bicuspid aortic stenosis. It occurs at the end of the isovolumetric contraction phase, just as the valve snaps open and blood begins to enter the aorta. As the valve becomes more calcified and less mobile with age, the click may disappear. It is best heard at the base or the apex and is followed by the characteristic crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur. It helps distinguish valvular stenosis from subvalvular conditions like HOCM.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: Hypertrophic Obstructive Cardiomyopathy (HOCM) is a {{c1::systolic}} murmur.
hint: The timing of the murmur in HOCM.
explanation: The murmur of HOCM is a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur, similar in shape to aortic stenosis. However, it is caused by functional obstruction of the left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) by the asymmetric hypertrophied septum and the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve (systolic anterior motion). It is best heard at the left lower sternal border and, unlike AS, does not radiate to the carotids. Its intensity is highly sensitive to changes in preload and afterload, making dynamic maneuvers essential for its identification.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: Handgrip maneuver {{c1::decreases}} the intensity of the Aortic Stenosis murmur.
hint: Effect of increased afterload on the flow across the aortic valve.
explanation: Performing a sustained handgrip increases systemic vascular resistance (afterload). This increase in pressure in the aorta makes it more difficult for the left ventricle to eject blood across the stenotic aortic valve. Consequently, the pressure gradient across the valve may decrease slightly and the velocity of the forward flow is reduced. This leads to a decrease in the turbulence and a corresponding softening of the crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur. This maneuver is useful to distinguish AS from mitral regurgitation, which gets louder with handgrip.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: Squatting {{c1::decreases}} the intensity of the HOCM murmur.
hint: Effect of increased preload/afterload on the HOCM obstruction.
explanation: Squatting increases both venous return (preload) and systemic vascular resistance (afterload). The increase in preload leads to a larger left ventricular end-diastolic volume. A more distended left ventricle keeps the hypertrophied septum further away from the mitral valve, thereby reducing the outflow tract obstruction. Additionally, increased afterload further distends the LV. Together, these effects result in a significant decrease in the intensity of the HOCM murmur, which is a classic finding used to differentiate it from aortic stenosis (which often gets louder with squatting).

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: A {{c1::bruit}} is a sound heard over a blood vessel (like the carotid), while a murmur is heard over the heart.
explanation: While both bruits and murmurs are caused by turbulent blood flow, 'murmur' is the term reserved for sounds originating within the heart chambers or across the heart valves. A 'bruit' is the sound heard when listening over a peripheral artery, such as the carotid, renal, or femoral arteries, usually indicating narrowing or atherosclerotic plaque. On the USMLE, you must distinguish between the radiation of an aortic stenosis murmur into the neck and a primary carotid bruit; an AS murmur is usually louder at the base of the heart, while a bruit is louder over the artery itself.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: The S2 heart sound is typically loudest at the {{c1::base}} of the heart.
hint: General region (top or bottom) where S2 is most prominent.
explanation: The 'base' of the heart refers to the superior aspect, where the great vessels (aorta and pulmonary artery) emerge. Because S2 is produced by the closure of the semilunar valves located in these vessels, the vibrations are most intense in the second intercostal spaces at the sternal borders. This is in contrast to S1, which is typically loudest at the 'apex' (the inferior-lateral aspect). Clinicians use the base to evaluate the split and intensity of the A2 and P2 components.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: Severe Mitral Stenosis leads to a {{c1::loud}} S1 sound.
hint: Intensity of S1 in the early stages of MS.
explanation: In mitral stenosis, the mitral valve leaflets are kept wide open until the very end of diastole due to the high pressure in the left atrium. When ventricular systole begins, the leaflets must travel a greater distance and snap shut with high force, resulting in a loud, 'tapping' S1. This is a classic finding in rheumatic mitral stenosis. However, as the disease progresses and the valve becomes heavily calcified and immobile, the S1 sound may eventually become soft or muffled because the leaflets can no longer move effectively.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: The Valsalva maneuver (Phase II) {{c1::increases}} the intensity of the Mitral Valve Prolapse (MVP) murmur.
hint: Effect of decreased preload on the MVP murmur.
explanation: The Valsalva maneuver increases intrathoracic pressure and decreases venous return, leading to a smaller left ventricular volume. In MVP, a smaller ventricle allows the redundant mitral valve leaflets to prolapse into the left atrium much earlier in the systolic phase. This results in an earlier mid-systolic click and a longer, louder systolic murmur. This dynamic change is a hallmark of MVP and is used clinically to confirm the diagnosis when a patient presents with a suspicious systolic click or murmur.

topic: Auscultation of the heart and dynamic murmurs
text: Carvallo's sign refers to the increase in {{c1::tricuspid regurgitation}} murmur intensity during inspiration.
hint: Named clinical sign for right-sided murmur change.
explanation: Carvallo's sign is a specific clinical finding used to identify tricuspid regurgitation (TR). During inspiration, the increase in venous return to the right heart increases the stroke volume of the right ventricle. This results in more blood being forced back through the incompetent tricuspid valve, Loudening the holosystolic murmur. It is an important diagnostic tool to differentiate TR from mitral regurgitation (MR), as MR does not typically increase with inspiration. This distinction is crucial for correctly identifying the valvular source of a holosystolic murmur.

text: {{c1::Aortic stenosis}} is a midsystolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur that is best heard at the right second intercostal space and radiates to the carotids.
hint: Commonly caused by age-related calcification or bicuspid valve.
explanation: Aortic stenosis results from the narrowing of the aortic valve, which creates a pressure gradient between the left ventricle and the aorta during systole. The murmur follows a crescendo-decrescendo pattern as blood flow increases and then decreases across the restricted orifice. Clinical manifestations often include the triad of syncope, angina, and dyspnea (SAD) as the obstruction progresses. It is often associated with a weak and delayed pulse, known as pulsus parvus et tardus.

text: The murmur of {{c1::Mitral regurgitation}} is a holosystolic, high-pitched 'blowing' murmur that often radiates to the axilla.
hint: Often occurs after myocardial infarction or due to MVP.
explanation: Mitral regurgitation occurs when the mitral valve fails to close properly, allowing blood to flow back into the left atrium during ventricular contraction. This backward flow creates a consistent pressure gradient throughout systole, resulting in a holosystolic (pansystolic) murmur. Common etiologies include chordae tendineae rupture post-MI, mitral valve prolapse, or left ventricular dilation. Chronic regurgitation leads to left atrial enlargement and eventual volume overload of the left ventricle.

text: {{c1::Tricuspid regurgitation}} is a holosystolic murmur heard at the left lower sternal border that increases in intensity with inspiration.
hint: Distinguish from MR by the response to the respiratory cycle.
explanation: Tricuspid regurgitation is characterized by the backflow of blood from the right ventricle into the right atrium during systole. The increase in venous return during inspiration (Carvallo sign) enhances the murmur's intensity, helping differentiate it from mitral regurgitation. It is frequently caused by right ventricular dilation, which may be secondary to pulmonary hypertension or left-sided heart failure. Clinically, it can present with prominent V waves in the jugular venous pulse and a pulsatile liver.

text: Mitral valve prolapse (MVP) typically presents with a {{c1::midsystolic click}} followed by a late systolic murmur.
hint: The click is caused by sudden tension in the chordae tendineae.
explanation: MVP involves the displacement of one or both mitral valve leaflets into the left atrium during systole, usually due to myxomatous degeneration. The midsystolic click occurs when the elongated chordae tendineae suddenly tighten as the leaflets reach their limit. This condition is often seen in connective tissue disorders like Marfan or Ehlers-Danlos syndromes. Maneuvers that decrease left ventricular volume, such as Valsalva, cause the click to occur earlier in systole.

text: A large {{c1::Ventricular septal defect (VSD)}} produces a harsh holosystolic murmur that is loudest at the left lower sternal border.
explanation: In a VSD, blood is shunted from the high-pressure left ventricle to the lower-pressure right ventricle during systole. The harshness of the murmur is inversely proportional to the size of the hole, as smaller defects create more turbulence. This left-to-right shunt increases pulmonary blood flow and can lead to pulmonary hypertension over time. If left untreated, the reversal of the shunt due to high pulmonary pressure is known as Eisenmenger syndrome.

text: {{c1::Aortic regurgitation}} is an early diastolic decrescendo murmur best heard at the left sternal border when the patient leans forward.
hint: Associated with wide pulse pressure and head bobbing.
explanation: Aortic regurgitation results from the failure of the aortic valve to close completely, allowing blood to leak back into the left ventricle during diastole. This causes an increase in stroke volume and a rapid decline in aortic pressure, leading to a wide pulse pressure. Common causes include aortic root dilation (e.g., Marfan syndrome, syphilis) or bicuspid aortic valve. The high stroke volume leads to various physical signs like 'water-hammer' pulses and Quincke's capillary pulsations.

text: The murmur of {{c1::Mitral stenosis}} is characterized by an opening snap followed by a mid-to-late diastolic rumble.
hint: Almost always a late sequela of rheumatic fever.
explanation: Mitral stenosis involves the narrowing of the mitral valve, which obstructs blood flow from the left atrium to the left ventricle during diastole. The opening snap occurs when the thickened, calcified valve leaflets reach their maximum excursion into the ventricle. The interval between the S2 sound and the opening snap correlates with the severity; a shorter interval indicates higher atrial pressure. Chronic stenosis leads to left atrial dilation, which significantly increases the risk of atrial fibrillation and pulmonary congestion.

text: A {{c1::Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA)}} produces a continuous machine-like murmur that is loudest at S2.
hint: Best heard at the left infraclavicular area.
explanation: A PDA represents a persistent connection between the aorta and the pulmonary artery that fails to close after birth. Because aortic pressure is higher than pulmonary pressure throughout both systole and diastole, the murmur is continuous. It is classically associated with congenital rubella infection and prematurity. Prostaglandin E1 keeps the ductus open, while indomethacin or ibuprofen (NSAIDs) can be used to facilitate its closure in neonates.

text: The intensity of right-sided heart murmurs (e.g., TR, PR) {{c1::increases}} during inspiration.
explanation: During inspiration, the decrease in intrathoracic pressure results in increased venous return to the right atrium and right ventricle. This higher volume of blood flowing across the right-sided valves enhances the turbulence and therefore the intensity of the associated murmurs. This physiological change is a key diagnostic tool used to differentiate right-sided murmurs from left-sided ones. Left-sided murmurs generally do not increase with inspiration and may actually decrease as blood is sequestered in the lungs.

text: The {{c1::Valsalva}} maneuver and standing decrease the intensity of most murmurs, but increase the intensity of HOCM and MVP.
explanation: Valsalva and standing both lead to decreased venous return (preload) to the heart. For most murmurs, like aortic stenosis, less blood flow across the valve results in a softer sound. However, in HOCM, decreased preload reduces the left ventricular size, allowing the hypertrophied septum to obstruct the outflow tract more easily, thus increasing the murmur. In MVP, the reduced volume causes the valve to prolapse earlier, lengthening the systolic murmur.

text: The {{c1::Handgrip}} maneuver increases the intensity of MR, AR, and VSD by increasing afterload.
explanation: Handgrip exercise increases systemic vascular resistance (afterload), which makes it harder for the left ventricle to eject blood into the aorta. This increased resistance forces more blood backward through a regurgitant mitral valve or across a ventricular septal defect, intensifying those murmurs. Conversely, it decreases the intensity of the aortic stenosis murmur because the pressure gradient across the aortic valve is reduced. It also helps differentiate HOCM from MR, as HOCM intensity decreases with increased afterload.

text: Squatting increases the intensity of most murmurs but {{c1::decreases}} the intensity of the HOCM murmur.
hint: Squatting increases both preload and afterload.
explanation: Squatting increases venous return (preload) and systemic vascular resistance (afterload) simultaneously. For HOCM, the increased ventricular volume (due to increased preload) helps to push the hypertrophied septum away from the mitral valve, reducing the outflow obstruction and the murmur. In most other cases, like AS or MR, the increased blood volume and backpressure make the murmurs louder. This maneuver is highly useful in distinguishing HOCM from aortic stenosis in a clinical setting.

text: The {{c1::Austin Flint}} murmur is a soft, mid-diastolic rumble heard at the apex in patients with severe aortic regurgitation.
hint: Caused by the regurgitant jet hitting the mitral valve.
explanation: The Austin Flint murmur is a functional murmur that occurs when the regurgitant jet from aortic insufficiency strikes the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve. This causes the mitral valve to partially close during diastole, creating a physiological state similar to mitral stenosis. It is distinguished from true mitral stenosis by the absence of an opening snap and the presence of other AR signs. Understanding this helps clinicians avoid misdiagnosing a secondary valvular problem in the setting of primary aortic disease.

text: In mitral stenosis, the time between the {{c1::S2}} and the opening snap decreases as the severity of the stenosis increases.
explanation: In mitral stenosis, the opening snap occurs when the left atrial pressure exceeds the left ventricular pressure at the start of diastole. As the stenosis becomes more severe, the left atrial pressure rises significantly, reaching the crossover point with ventricular pressure much earlier. Consequently, the mitral valve is forced open sooner after S2 (aortic/pulmonic valve closure). A shorter S2-to-opening-snap interval is therefore a reliable indicator of high left atrial pressure and severe valvular narrowing.

text: {{c1::Pulmonic stenosis}} presents as a midsystolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the left upper sternal border that may radiate to the left shoulder.
hint: Often associated with Tetralogy of Fallot.
explanation: Pulmonic stenosis is an obstruction of blood flow from the right ventricle into the pulmonary artery. The murmur is similar in quality to aortic stenosis but is heard best in the pulmonic area and increases with inspiration (Carvallo sign). It is a classic component of the Tetralogy of Fallot, along with VSD, overriding aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy. Severe stenosis can lead to right heart failure and is often congenital in origin rather than acquired.

text: {{c1::Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM)}} produces a harsh systolic ejection murmur that is loudest at the left lower sternal border and does NOT radiate to the carotids.
hint: Common cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes.
explanation: The HOCM murmur is caused by dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction as the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve moves toward the hypertrophied septum (SAM). Unlike aortic stenosis, this murmur does not radiate to the neck and responds differently to physical maneuvers. Decreasing preload (Valsalva) makes it louder, while increasing preload (squatting) makes it softer. This is a critical distinction for preventing sudden death in patients with undiagnosed cardiac hypertrophy during physical exertion.

text: The murmur of {{c1::Tricuspid stenosis}} is a mid-diastolic rumble heard at the left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration.
hint: Often seen alongside mitral stenosis in rheumatic heart disease.
explanation: Tricuspid stenosis is a narrowing of the tricuspid valve orifice, typically caused by rheumatic heart disease. Similar to mitral stenosis, it produces a diastolic rumble, but it is located more medially and increases in intensity when the patient inhales. This increase during inspiration is due to the augmented venous return to the right heart. It often leads to elevated right atrial pressures, which may present as prominent 'a' waves in the jugular venous pulse and peripheral edema.

text: A {{c1::Graham Steell}} murmur is a high-pitched, blowing early diastolic decrescendo murmur caused by pulmonary regurgitation.
explanation: The Graham Steell murmur occurs when severe pulmonary hypertension causes dilation of the pulmonary artery ring, leading to pulmonary valve incompetence. It is heard at the left sternal border and is virtually indistinguishable from aortic regurgitation by sound alone. However, the presence of signs of pulmonary hypertension (like a loud P2) and the murmur's increase with inspiration point toward a pulmonic origin. It is a sign of significant underlying pulmonary vascular disease or secondary right-sided heart strain.

text: Aortic stenosis can lead to {{c1::pulsus parvus et tardus}}, which refers to a pulse that is weak and delayed.
explanation: Pulsus parvus et tardus is a classic physical exam finding in severe aortic stenosis, reflecting the slowed and diminished ejection of blood through the narrowed valve. The 'parvus' (small) refers to the decreased stroke volume and pulse pressure, while 'tardus' (late) refers to the prolonged time it takes for the arterial pulse to reach its peak. This is best palpated in the carotid arteries. Its presence suggests significant valvular obstruction and often correlates with a high pressure gradient across the aortic valve.

text: The {{c1::Carvallo}} sign refers to the increase in the intensity of a tricuspid regurgitation murmur during inspiration.
hint: Used to differentiate TR from MR.
explanation: Carvallo's sign is a clinical maneuver used to identify right-sided heart murmurs. By having the patient inspire deeply, the clinician increases the negative intrathoracic pressure, which draws more blood into the right ventricle. The resulting increase in stroke volume through the tricuspid valve makes the murmur of tricuspid regurgitation louder. This sign is highly specific for right-sided pathology. In contrast, mitral regurgitation either stays the same or slightly decreases in intensity during the same maneuver.

text: A {{c1::bicuspid aortic valve}} is the most common cause of aortic stenosis in patients younger than 65.
explanation: While senile calcification is the primary cause of aortic stenosis in the elderly, a bicuspid aortic valve accelerates this process. Patients born with two leaflets instead of three experience increased mechanical stress and turbulence, leading to premature calcification and fibrosis. This typically results in symptomatic stenosis in the 5th or 6th decade of life. It is also frequently associated with other cardiovascular anomalies, such as coarctation of the aorta or aortic root dilation.

text: In severe aortic regurgitation, the {{c1::Water-hammer pulse}} (Corrigan pulse) is a rapidly rising and falling arterial pulse.
explanation: The Water-hammer pulse is caused by the large stroke volume of the left ventricle being rapidly ejected into the aorta followed by a quick regurgitation of that blood back into the ventricle. This results in a sharp, high-amplitude upstroke and a sudden collapse of the arterial pressure. It is one of the many 'peripheral signs' of chronic AR that reflect the significantly widened pulse pressure. This finding is usually most prominent in the radial or carotid arteries when the limb is elevated.

text: Rheumatic heart disease is the most common cause of {{c1::Mitral stenosis}} worldwide.
hint: Occurs years after an infection with Group A Strep.
explanation: Acute rheumatic fever can cause pancarditis, but the most significant long-term consequence is chronic valvular scarring, particularly of the mitral valve. This process involves commissural fusion and chordae shortening, which narrows the valve opening. Over decades, this leads to the classic 'fish-mouth' appearance of the valve and clinical mitral stenosis. Although less common in developed nations due to antibiotic use, it remains a major cause of heart failure and stroke in many parts of the world.

text: The murmur of {{c1::Atrial septal defect (ASD)}} is often a midsystolic flow murmur over the pulmonic area with a fixed split S2.
hint: Caused by increased flow, not the defect itself.
explanation: An ASD allows blood to shunt from the left atrium to the right atrium, which increases the total volume of blood ejected by the right ventricle. This extra volume causes a 'flow murmur' across the pulmonic valve during systole, mimicking pulmonic stenosis. The classic 'fixed split S2' occurs because the increased right-sided volume delays pulmonic valve closure, and this delay does not change with respiration because the shunt equalizes pressures. Long-term shunting can lead to right-sided heart failure and pulmonary hypertension.

text: {{c1::Mitral valve prolapse}} is often associated with the 'billowing' of the valve leaflets into the atrium due to myxomatous degeneration.
hint: Commonly benign, but can lead to MR.
explanation: Myxomatous degeneration involves the accumulation of dermatan sulfate within the valve leaflets, making them thick and redundant. During systole, the high pressure in the left ventricle pushes these weakened leaflets back into the left atrium beyond the annular plane. This 'billowing' creates the characteristic click when the chordae are stretched. While often asymptomatic, it can progress to significant mitral regurgitation, infective endocarditis, or even chordal rupture. It is the most common valvular abnormality in the general population.

text: The murmur of {{c1::Aortic stenosis}} is often described as having a 'diamond-shaped' configuration on phonocardiogram.
explanation: The 'diamond shape' describes the rise and fall of the murmur's intensity as the pressure gradient between the ventricle and aorta changes during systole. In early systole, the gradient increases (crescendo), and as the ventricle begins to relax and empty, the gradient decreases (decrescendo). The timing of the peak intensity can indicate the severity of the stenosis; a later peak often suggests more severe obstruction. This term is synonymous with the crescendo-decrescendo description used in clinical practice.

text: In patients with aortic regurgitation, {{c1::De Musset}} sign is characterized by rhythmic head bobbing in sync with the heartbeat.
hint: A physical sign of wide pulse pressure.
explanation: De Musset sign is one of the numerous eponymous physical findings associated with severe, chronic aortic insufficiency. It occurs because the massive stroke volume and wide pulse pressure cause a visible jarring of the head with each systolic contraction. Like other signs such as Traube's sign or Muller's sign, it reflects the hyperdynamic circulation. While interesting historically, these signs are less commonly emphasized today as echocardiography provides a more definitive assessment of valvular severity.

text: A diastolic murmur heard at the left lower sternal border that is caused by {{c1::Syphilitic aortitis}} is due to aortic root dilation.
explanation: Tertiary syphilis can cause vasa vasorum inflammation (endarteritis obliterans), leading to destruction of the aortic wall and aneurysmal dilation of the aortic root. As the root dilates, the aortic valve leaflets are pulled apart, preventing them from coapting properly during diastole. This results in aortic regurgitation. Because the pathology is in the root rather than the leaflets, the murmur is often loudest at the right sternal border. This condition also carries a risk of coronary ostial stenosis and aortic dissection.

text: A holosystolic murmur that is heard best at the apex and is louder with {{c1::Squatting}} suggests mitral regurgitation.
explanation: Squatting increases systemic vascular resistance, which increases the afterload on the left ventricle. In the setting of mitral regurgitation, this increased resistance to forward flow into the aorta encourages more blood to regurgitate back through the incompetent mitral valve into the left atrium. This increases the turbulence and volume of the regurgitant jet, thereby intensifying the holosystolic murmur. Squatting also increases venous return, which adds to the volume available for regurgitation, further accentuating the sound.

text: The intensity of the {{c1::VSD}} murmur typically decreases with the administration of vasodilators like nitroglycerin.
explanation: Vasodilators reduce systemic vascular resistance (afterload), making it easier for the left ventricle to pump blood into the aorta. Since there is less resistance to forward flow, the pressure gradient driving blood from the left ventricle to the right ventricle across the VSD is reduced. As the shunt volume decreases, the turbulence—and thus the intensity of the holosystolic murmur—diminishes. This principle is used both diagnostically and therapeutically to manage the workload of the heart in shunting conditions.

text: {{c1::Infective endocarditis}} can cause sudden onset of new murmurs, most commonly mitral or aortic regurgitation.
